title: Giulia: The Poison Queen of Palermo by Jennifer Nettles at PAC NYC #g...
transcript: Giulia: The Poison Queen of Palermo is a tale of female rage and revenge, dripping with vocal charisma but lacking in specificity. Written by and starring country musician Jennifer Nettles, it's based on the life of Giulia Tofana, an Italian woman in the 1600s who ran an apothecary where she supplied poison for women to off their abusive husbands with. In this musical, her first kill is an act of fight or flight against her own husband in order to protect her daughter. The setting and character motivations up to this point are clear — society is suffocatingly patriarchal, and Giulia's community is full of battered women, all desperate for agency and fed up with their male counterparts. A basic story progresses, though not in a particularly surprising or dramatically notable way. What is notable is the electric female ensemble and their searing defiance against the patriarchy. There are plenty of great moments sprinkled throughout this rather lengthy musical, many of which can be attributed to stellar vocals and the melodically rich score by Nettles. However, the lyrics leave much to be desired. As they're incredibly plain, they sometimes work in the more conversational songs, but more often than not feel distractingly direct. The piece as a whole operates on a single wavelength — it sounds cohesive, yet it runs at a mezzo forte to forte the vast majority of the time. And when almost every song has the gusto of an 11 o'clock number, the experience becomes arduous. Overall, I think if the piece were more tonally and dynamically balanced and prioritized character development, especially in the titular role, it would hit much harder. Otherwise, the potency you'd expect from a musical about a “poison queen” falls a little flat. With that, another program for my collection.
